case_study_insert.main_stem: Marlow Technical Textiles (MTT) is a private limited company in the textiles sector, manufacturing flame-retardant and recycled-fibre fabrics for workwear, transport and rail interiors across global markets, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 2013 by Elena Marchetti, MTT operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. MTT plans to invest $720,000 in a digital jacquard weaving loom with computer-aided manufacturing, financed by a $450,000 bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $432,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.60 a unit and a selling price of $13.00, and currently produces 110,000 units a year. MTT faces an HR problem: absenteeism in the weaving hall has reached 12%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — October 2026: MTT surveyed 140 procurement managers at workwear and transport manufacturers. 58% now require recycled-content certified fabrics, and 44% would accept a price premium of up to 8%. 61% identified flame-retardant certification as a decisive buying factor. Customer complaints about dye consistency fell from 14 to 6 per month after the new finishing process. Orders from 3 new export clients totalled $180,000 in the quarter. On-the-job training is informal; 22 of 85 staff need updated computer-aided manufacturing training; off-the-job training courses cost $1,000 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Marlow Technical Textiles as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.2% to 6.1%, increasing borrowing costs for variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.12 to $12.90 per hour from April 2027. (3) Cotton and polyester input costs have risen 10.5% year-on-year, textile price inflation is running at 6.5%, while demand for certified sustainable fabrics grew 7.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: MTT plans to finance part of its digital jacquard loom purchase with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for MTT of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs MTT nothing in interest or repayments, protecting cash flow and profit margin while it already carries fixed costs of $432,000 a year and a $450,000 bank loan. Money not paid as interest can absorb the 10.5% rise in cotton and polyester input costs without raising the $13.00 selling price for workwear and transport clients. It also avoids lender covenants that could constrain how Elena Marchetti runs the loom programme.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral risk attached to a bank loan, so the $270,000 does not put the new $720,000 jacquard loom at risk of repossession if export orders such as the three clients worth $180,000 in a quarter prove slower to repeat. It also keeps Elena Marchetti's ownership and creative control intact, with no lender able to dictate how the flat structure or laissez-faire teams run the weaving hall. This flexibility matters while absenteeism is 12% and the business adapts to computer-aided manufacturing. Elena Marchetti also keeps full creative and commercial control while the loom beds in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Marlow Technical Textiles and its loom investment decision.

questions.question_text: MTT is launching its recycled-fibre fabric range. Consider exhibiting at an international textile trade fair, advertising in technical textile journals, or a targeted LinkedIn campaign aimed at procurement managers. Which should MTT choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade fair exhibition: An international textile trade fair puts MTT's flame-retardant, recycled-fibre fabrics directly in front of procurement managers, allows tactile demonstrations of weave quality and fire certification, and can create relationships that generate repeat orders. However, stand space, travel and samples are expensive, events happen only a few times a year, and follow-up conversion from a 85-person firm is uncertain against larger rival mills.

Technical journal advertising: Journals read by workwear and transport buyers reach exactly the decision-makers MTT surveyed, build technical credibility with certification claims and offer repetition across issues at low cost. Readership is passive, response is hard to measure, and print lead times do not suit the 7.1% growth in demand for sustainable fabrics or the momentum behind MTT's new export clients.

LinkedIn campaign: A LinkedIn campaign aimed at the 140 procurement managers in MTT's research targets the 58% who require recycled-content certified fabrics and the 44% who accept a price premium of up to 8%, with measurable clicks, sample requests and cost per lead. It scales internationally for export growth and suits MTT's design-led flat culture, though it needs consistent technical content and rapid follow-up to convert interest.

Recommendation: MTT should choose a targeted LinkedIn campaign, reinforced by one international textile trade fair each year. It speaks directly to the certified-sustainability segment at a fraction of exhibition cost and supports export growth. Journal advertising is rejected as too passive to win specification decisions, and exhibiting alone is rejected as too expensive and infrequent for a firm funding a $720,000 loom with a $450,000 bank loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of MTT with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of MTT with a well-justified recommendation explaining why journals and exhibition-only approaches are rejected.

questions.question_text: MTT's absenteeism in the weaving hall has reached 12%. Explain two benefits for MTT of using laissez-faire leadership to improve motivation among its weavers and designers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives MTT's skilled weavers and fabric designers real autonomy over how they set looms, plan weaves and solve dye-consistency issues, satisfying esteem and self-actualisation needs. Autonomously motivated craftspeople typically show higher job satisfaction and lower absenteeism, which is exactly what MTT needs to pull the weaving hall's 12% rate down without heavy-handed supervision that would clash with its flat culture. MTT should pair this autonomy with monthly informal one-to-ones to catch disengagement early.

Point 2: Giving teams room to experiment encourages ownership of quality and innovation, such as reducing dye-consistency complaints from 14 to 6 per month through their own finishing adjustments. Higher commitment also lowers the risk of losing key specialists to rival mills, protects output of 110,000 units a year and supports the creative pipeline needed for the recycled-fibre range that 58% of surveyed buyers now require, all while Elena Marchetti retains strategic direction from the centre and can step in quickly if laissez-faire freedom starts costing delivery deadlines.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MTT's absenteeism, quality and recycled-fibre strategy.

questions.question_text: MTT must train 22 staff on the new computer-aided manufacturing loom. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at an external centre. Which should MTT choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training beside the new jacquard loom is directly relevant to MTT's exact weave programs and recycled yarns, costs nothing in course fees and keeps the weaving hall producing while staff learn, which protects output of 110,000 units a year and the $180,000 quarterly orders from new export clients. Drawbacks are that informal coaching under laissez-faire leadership makes skills uneven across the 22 staff, bad habits can spread, and there is no certificate for procurement managers who demand evidence of computer-aided manufacturing competence.

Off-the-job training: External computer-aided manufacturing courses at $1,000 per employee cost $22,000 for the 22 staff, affordable beside the $720,000 loom investment, and deliver structured, standardised skills plus certificates MTT can show buyers requiring recycled-content documentation. Staff are removed from the weaving hall for days at a time, however, deepening the disruption caused by 12% absenteeism, and generic content needs adaptation to MTT's specific loom, so on-site follow-up would still be required.

Decision: MTT should choose off-the-job training for all 22 staff, combined with short on-the-job mentoring from the fastest learners afterwards. Off-the-job certification is the only route that gives every operator the same verified competence quickly, supports the buyer audit trail and complements the loom's digital programming. Pure on-the-job training is rejected as too inconsistent for a laissez-faire environment where nobody is centrally enforcing standards, and it would leave MTT unable to demonstrate certified capability to the 58% of buyers specifying recycled-content fabrics. The $22,000 course cost is covered by contribution on well under 5,000 units of output, and faster verified competence should help MTT hold the dye-consistency gains behind the fall from 14 to 6 complaints a month.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to MTT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of MTT.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of MTT with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, certification and buyer audit needs.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how MTT's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $432,000 ÷ ($13.00 − $7.60) = $432,000 ÷ $5.40 = 80,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 80,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $13.00 − $7.60 = $5.40. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.40.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways MTT's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 80,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 110,000 units to confirm a margin of safety of 30,000 units, judging whether the recycled-fibre launch can absorb demand fluctuations before the loom becomes loss-making.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.40 lets MTT model the 44% of buyers willing to pay a premium of up to 8%; raising the price to $14.04 would lift contribution to $6.44, quantifying the reward for certification marketing.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $432,000 and contribution per unit helps managers check the $450,000 bank loan for the $720,000 loom can be serviced before any further investment is committed.
4. Managers can use average total cost ($432,000 ÷ 110,000 units + $7.60 = $11.53 a unit) to benchmark quarterly weaving performance, tackle the 12% absenteeism through productivity figures (110,000 ÷ 85 staff ≈ 1,294 units per worker) and renegotiate cotton and polyester supply as input costs rise 10.5%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 80,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.40 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 30,000 units versus 110,000-unit output; premium pricing modelling at 8% against $432,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $720,000 loom; and unit-cost benchmarking at $11.53 alongside labour productivity to tackle absenteeism and 10.5% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate MTT's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has MTT's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.42 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.67 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.18 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $140,000 inventories + $175,000 trade receivables + $55,000 cash = $370,000; 2025 current assets = $110,000 + $195,000 + $70,000 = $375,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $370,000 ÷ $260,000 = 1.42; 2025 = $375,000 ÷ $225,000 = 1.67. Cover excluding inventories 2024 = ($370,000 − $140,000) ÷ $260,000 = $230,000 ÷ $260,000 = 0.88; 2025 = ($375,000 − $110,000) ÷ $225,000 = $265,000 ÷ $225,000 = 1.18.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. Short-term cover improved from 1.42 to 1.67 as inventories were reduced from $140,000 to $110,000 and liabilities fell from $260,000 to $225,000. The tougher measure excluding inventories moved from 0.88 to 1.18, so MTT no longer relies on selling fabric stock to meet short-term debts, which is vital while it services a $450,000 bank loan for the $720,000 jacquard loom. However, trade receivables rose from $175,000 to $195,000, tying up cash; if workwear and transport clients delay payment, the stronger position could weaken. Inventories of $110,000 must also still cover seasonal peaks in flame-retardant fabric demand.

Conclusion: MTT's financial position has improved. Both liquidity measures rose (1.42 to 1.67 and 0.88 to 1.18), and the improvement does not depend on stock. The main residual risk is rising receivables, so MTT should tighten credit control with export clients while the loom beds in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether MTT's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for MTT of launching a recycled-fibre fabric range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A recycled-fibre range directly answers the 58% of surveyed procurement managers who require recycled-content certified fabrics and the 44% who would accept a price premium of up to 8%, allowing MTT to lift price toward $14.04 and contribution above $5.40 a unit. It differentiates MTT in a commoditised textiles market, supports the demand for certified sustainable fabrics growing at 7.1% and helps win specification on workwear and transport contracts, including the three new export clients worth $180,000 in a quarter.

Disadvantage: Recycled fibres can cost more and behave less predictably in spinning and dyeing, raising the $7.60 variable cost and risking a return of dye-consistency complaints before the new finishing process stabilises. Certification audits and recycled-content documentation add cost and admin to an 85-person business with 12% absenteeism, and if flame-retardant performance is compromised, the decisive certification advantage for 61% of buyers would be destroyed, damaging orders and MTT's technical reputation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to MTT's research data, costs and certification strategy.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.1%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in input costs will affect MTT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.2% to 6.1%): MTT's $450,000 bank loan, if variable-rate, rises by 0.9%, adding about $4,050 a year to interest costs and slightly lifting the fixed-cost burden above $432,000. Higher rates may also make export clients slower to place large orders and raise the cost of future borrowing for the $720,000 loom. The direct impact is modest and can be capped by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $12.90 per hour): MTT employs 85 staff, mostly weavers and finishers. If the lowest-paid 25 operatives move from $12.12 to $12.90, each gains about $1,560 a year, or roughly $39,000 across the group. Skilled weavers and designers earn well above the minimum, so the total wage bill rises by far less than 6.4%, though the 12% absenteeism makes any pay friction harder to absorb.

Input cost inflation (10.5% cotton and polyester): Cotton and polyester dominate the $7.60 variable cost at roughly $4.50 per unit. A 10.5% rise adds about $0.47 per unit; at 110,000 units that is roughly $52,000 a year, directly cutting the $5.40 contribution per unit and pressuring the $13.00 price for workwear and transport clients.

Conclusion: The 10.5% rise in cotton and polyester input costs will have the greatest impact. It repeatedly reduces contribution on every metre of fabric sold, totalling roughly $52,000 a year, the largest cash exposure of the three. The wage increase is the second concern at roughly $39,000 a year, while the interest-rate rise costs only about $4,050 a year and can be managed by fixing the loan rate; all three reinforce the case for the recycled-fibre premium strategy and tighter cost control in the weaving hall.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to MTT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on MTT's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of MTT with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
